strengths: The paper addresses a critical limitation of existing perturbation prediction models—namely, the lack of explicit inductive biases for coordinated, module-level gene programs—by proposing a principled framework spanning module induction, structured attention, and generative flow matching.

The proposed Gene-Relation Clustering (GRC) via balanced optimal transport effectively fuses foundation-model semantic representations with high-confidence PPI networks, avoiding both the limitations of purely static graphs and unstructured flat token sequences.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and rigorous, benchmarking against 13 state-of-the-art baselines across multiple paradigms (foundation models, graph-based methods, and generative models) on both Norman (additive and holdout splits) and Replogle RPE1 benchmarks, demonstrating consistent and meaningful gains.

The experimental section provides comprehensive ablations covering module partitioning strategies, clustering balance constraints, loss components, embedding choices, and structural hyperparameters, supported by error bars across random seeds.

The paper provides biological interpretability through Reactome pathway enrichment of induced modules and attention shift analyses that align with known biological mechanisms (e.g., NOL8 and KCTD10 knockdowns).
weaknesses: Draft artifacts remain in the figures; specifically, Figure 4 on page 6 contains unedited placeholder text in Chinese ('聚类散点图（然后每个圈给个名字）对比一下PPI前后') which impairs presentation quality.

In Algorithm 3, the structure-aware regularizers (Cluster Correlation Alignment and Pathway-informed OT) rely on caching ground-truth target statistics for condition p during training. The manuscript could more explicitly clarify how the flow field regularized by seen target statistics generalizes to zero-shot holdout perturbations during inference where no target statistics are available.

The exact mathematical formulation for extracting module-level differential attention (ΔAttention in Figure 4) from the Perceiver-style cross-attention layers is not explicitly formalized in Section 2.2 or Section 3.4.

While the benchmarks chosen (Norman K562 and Replogle RPE1) are standard, the evaluation remains restricted to two cell lines; evaluating across more varied tissues or cross-cell-type transfer would further substantiate claims of broad applicability.

strengths: Well-motivated biological inductive bias: The paper addresses a known fundamental challenge in single-cell perturbation modeling—that transcriptional responses act via coordinated gene programs rather than independent genes or rigid, static graphs—by proposing a module-inductive architecture.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: The proposed method (scBIG) is evaluated against 13 diverse and competitive baselines spanning statistical models, single-cell foundation models (scGPT, scFoundation, GeneCompass, CellFM), graph-based networks (GEARS, CellOracle, GraphVCI), and continuous generative models (CellFlow, STATE, samsVAE) across both combinatorial (additive) and zero-shot holdout splits.

Solid empirical performance: Across multiple established metrics (e.g., Pearson correlation on all genes and top DEGs, directional accuracy, and perturbation discrimination score), scBIG demonstrates consistent and meaningful gains over existing state-of-the-art baselines on both Norman and Replogle RPE1 datasets.

Thorough ablation studies and biological validation: The authors systematically ablate clustering methods (GRC vs. k-means), cluster size constraints (balanced vs. unbalanced), individual biological loss components, and choice of embeddings (ESM2 vs. GeneCompass). They also provide biological sanity checks via Reactome pathway enrichment and attention shift analyses.
weaknesses: Presentation and drafting oversight: In Figure 4 (page 6), unedited draft comments/placeholders in Chinese are visible within the figure canvas ('聚类散点图（然后每个圈给个名字） 对比一下PPI前后'). Such oversights undermine the polish and rigor expected of a top-tier conference submission.

Rigid balanced module size assumption: In GRC (Section 2.1), the optimal transport formulation enforces strictly balanced hard clusters (|c_k| = G/K ≈ 64 genes). Biological pathways and co-regulatory programs vary widely in size (ranging from a handful of genes to several hundreds); artificially constraining all modules to equal cardinality may split large natural pathways or force unrelated genes into smaller pathways.

Missing details on combinatorial perturbation conditioning: Section 2.3 notes that perturbation condition c is derived from ESM2 embeddings, but the manuscript does not clearly describe how combinatorial/dual-gene perturbations (e.g., paired knockouts in the Norman dataset) are mathematically composed into c (e.g., sum, mean, concatenation, or cross-attention).

Computational overhead of training-time ODE integration: In Algorithm 3 (lines 16–18), computing the consistency losses (L_corr and L_pathway) requires numerically solving the ODE endpoint (ẑ_1 = ODESOLVE(z_0, v_θ, c)) at every training step. While per-step timing is benchmarked, the number of solver integration steps, backward-pass differentiation method (e.g., adjoint vs. backpropagation through solver), and total wall-clock training time across 500,000 iterations require more transparency.

strengths: Clear biological and methodological motivation: The paper addresses a major limitation in single-cell perturbation modeling—namely, the gene-independence assumption of flat representations and the rigidity of static graph priors—by proposing module-inductive representations that capture coordinated gene programs.

Well-structured and coherent technical framework: The combination of Gene-Relation Clustering (GRC) via balanced optimal transport, the Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder (GCAE) via a Perceiver-style bottleneck, conditional flow matching, and structure-aware regularizers (cluster correlation alignment and pathway OT) is technically sound and well-integrated.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate scBIG against 13 baselines spanning four distinct paradigms (foundation models, graph-based methods, latent generative models, and statistical baselines) across two widely used benchmarks (Norman and Replogle RPE1) under both combinatorial additive and zero-shot holdout settings.

Extensive ablations and interpretability: The submission includes thorough ablation analyses (evaluating clustering strategies, cluster size constraints, loss functions, embedding types, and efficiency/runtime trade-offs) as well as biological validation through pathway enrichment and attention shift case studies (e.g., NOL8 and KCTD10 knockdowns).
weaknesses: Biological artificiality of strictly balanced cluster sizes: In GRC, the algorithm enforces equal cluster sizes (|c_k| = G/K) via capacity-constrained rounding to facilitate chunked tensor processing. In reality, biological pathways and co-regulated modules vary dramatically in size; artificially forcing uniform cluster sizes risks either fragmenting large functional complexes or packing spurious genes into small modules.

Drafting artifact in Figure 4: Figure 4 contains unedited draft annotations in Chinese ('聚类散点图（然后每个圈给个名字） 对比一下PPI前后') above the subplots, which detracts from the professional presentation of the manuscript.

Clarification on test-time inference vs. training alignment: In Algorithm 3, the cluster correlation and pathway alignment losses rely on caching ground-truth perturbation statistics (R_gt*(p) and y_gt*(p)). While testing uses the learned vector field to integrate from control to t=1 without access to these targets, the text should more explicitly clarify the transition from training-time regularized trajectories to zero-shot test evaluation.

Evaluation restricted to top 2,000 HVGs: While standard in the perturbation prediction literature, restricting the gene space to ~2,000 highly variable genes leaves open questions regarding how well the balanced OT clustering and Perceiver encoder scale when applied to genome-wide expression profiles (15,000–20,000 genes).

strengths: Strong biological motivation: Modeling gene expression changes at the level of coordinated functional modules rather than isolated, independent gene tokens or rigid static graphs addresses a key limitation of existing perturbation prediction methods.

Well-engineered and principled architecture: The integration of Gene-Relation Clustering (GRC via balanced optimal transport combining foundation model semantics and PPI priors), Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder (GCAE with Perceiver-style bottleneck attention), conditional flow matching, and structure-aware alignment (correlation and pathway-informed OT) is coherent and technically sound.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The paper benchmarks against 13 representative baselines across four distinct paradigms on multiple Perturb-seq datasets (Norman, Replogle RPE1), different generalization regimes (additive combinations, zero-shot holdout), and chemical perturbations (ComboSciPlex), consistently showing clear performance gains on point, DEG-specific, and distributional metrics.

In-depth biological validation and interpretability: The authors perform post-hoc Reactome enrichment audits, identify stable cross-module coactivation patterns, and provide mechanistic case studies demonstrating biologically plausible attention shifts under specific gene knockdowns (e.g., NOL8 and KCTD10).

Thorough ablation and scalability analysis: The manuscript includes detailed ablations on clustering strategies, encoder choices, loss terms, embedding choices, and structural hyperparameters, as well as wall-clock runtime and memory profiling across different gene set sizes.
weaknesses: Artificial balanced cluster constraint: Enforcing strictly equal-sized clusters (|c_k| = G/K) via capacity-constrained rounding is an architectural compromise for chunk-wise computation that contradicts the biological reality of highly variable pathway and gene program sizes.

Computational overhead of training-time ODE integration: In Algorithm 3, computing the decoded endpoint x̂_1 for the correlation and pathway alignment losses requires an ODE solve at every training iteration, which can be computationally heavy and limit scalability to very large cellular datasets.
Minor presentation oversight: Page 8 contains unedited drafting notes / placeholder text in Chinese above Figure 4 ('聚类散点图（然后每个圈给个名字） 对比一下PPI前后'), which should be cleaned up in the final version.

strengths: Compelling and biologically well-founded motivation: explicitly addressing the limitation of flat, gene-wise representations and rigid static biological graphs by inducing coordinated functional modules directly through foundation-model semantics and PPI priors.

Sound and elegant architectural design: integrating balanced optimal transport clustering (GRC), a Perceiver-style bottleneck encoder (GCAE) for scalable inter-module interaction, and conditional flow matching with biological structure-preserving losses (cluster correlation and pathway-informed OT).

Extensive and rigorous empirical validation: the proposed method is evaluated against 13 strong baselines across multiple paradigms (foundation models, graph-based methods, generative models, and linear baselines) on diverse benchmarks (Norman additive/holdout, Replogle RPE1, and ComboSciPlex drug perturbations), showing consistent and statistically significant gains.

Thorough ablations and biological analysis: comprehensive ablations validate the necessity of each architectural component and loss term, supplemented by meaningful mechanistic analyses (pathway enrichment, cross-module coactivation, and differential attention shifts) that demonstrate biological interpretability.
weaknesses: The strictly balanced module partition (|c_k| = G/K) enforced by capacity-constrained optimal transport is an artificial architectural constraint; biological gene programs and pathways vary significantly in size, and enforcing equal partition sizes may split coherent pathways or force unrelated genes together.

Computational complexity of the end-to-end alignment objectives during training: computing L_corr and L_pathway requires integrating the ODE trajectory (via ODESolve) to obtain the predicted endpoint z_hat_1 and decoding it to full gene space at each training iteration, which adds optimization overhead and dependency on ODE solver parameters.

Heavy reliance on multiple external databases and pre-trained models (GeneCompass embeddings, STRING PPI networks, Reactome pathway annotations, ESM2 perturbation embeddings), making the framework somewhat complex with many interacting components and dependent on the quality/coverage of external biological resources.

strengths: Strong biological motivation: The paper tackles a fundamental limitation of existing perturbation prediction methods—namely, the treatment of genes as flat, independent tokens or reliance on rigid, static graphs—by explicitly incorporating a module-level inductive bias reflecting coordinated transcriptional programs.

Well-engineered and principled methodology: The three-stage framework (Gene-Relation Clustering via optimal transport, hierarchical Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder with Perceiver bottleneck, and conditional flow matching with dual structure-aware regularizers) is coherent, elegant, and addresses both computational tractability and biological fidelity.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The authors benchmark scBIG against 13 diverse baselines (spanning statistical baselines, single-cell foundation models, graph-based methods, and generative flow/diffusion models) across multiple datasets (Norman, Replogle RPE1, and ComboSciPlex) and challenging generalization splits (additive dual-perturbations, zero-shot holdouts, and cross-cell-line transfer).

Detailed ablation studies and biological interpretability: The paper includes extensive ablations (probing clustering algorithms, encoders, loss components, loss weights, and gene embeddings), paired statistical significance tests, and biologically grounded case studies (e.g., Reactome pathway enrichment audits and mechanistic attention shift analyses for NOL8 and KCTD10 knockouts).
weaknesses: Unnatural equal-size cluster constraint: The Gene-Relation Clustering enforces strictly balanced partition sizes (|c_k| = G/K) via capacity-constrained rounding to facilitate chunk-wise attention. While practically convenient for tensor operations, this is biologically artificial, as true gene regulatory programs and canonical pathways vary substantially in size.

Heavy reliance on external multi-source priors: The framework concurrently depends on GeneCompass single-cell foundation model embeddings, STRING PPI interaction networks, ESM2 protein language model embeddings, and Reactome pathway databases. This multi-prior reliance limits plug-and-play adaptability to non-model organisms, poorly annotated cell types, or conditions where static priors are incomplete or biased.

Computational overhead of ODE integration during Stage II training: Enforcing the structure-aware losses (L_corr and L_pathway) requires solving the full ODE trajectory to generate decoded endpoints within the training loop. Although cached targets and small batch configurations mitigate wall-clock time, backpropagating through ODE integration can introduce substantial GPU memory overhead and scaling challenges to whole-transcriptome screens.
Minor presentation polish issue: Figure 4 on page 8 includes unedited Chinese draft placeholder annotations ('聚类散点图（然后每个圈给个名字） 对比一下PPI前后'), which should be removed in the final camera-ready revision.
